headline: Cockenoe After Dark: Stripers Slide Into the Rocks While Blues Run the Daylight
subhead: With the Sound sitting warm from Greenwich to Bridgeport, the reef game splits in two — bass at night, everything else on the moving tide.
body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday to skip the daytime drift over Cockenoe and instead set up on the east end drop-off two hours before dark — the last of the ebb sliding into the bottom of the flood, right where the reef falls from eight feet into eighteen. That's the kind of decision you have to make right now. Kings Point is reading close to 71 degrees, and by mid-afternoon the shallows off Greenwich Point and the flats around Sheffield Island are running warmer than that. Bass don't like it. They've gone underground during daylight — holding deep on the structure, sitting on current seams, refusing to commit until the sun's off the water. You can beat your head against that with a bucktail at noon, or you can fish around it. I fish around it.

That means bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig, 3/0 circle hook, fished tight to the rockpile on the drop at Cockenoe's east end, or drifted eels through the Sheffield Island channel on the last two hours of outgoing into the top of the flood. Greenwich Point's rocks are doing the same thing after dark — current pushing bait against structure, stripers sliding up out of the deeper holes to work it. Nothing has been easy about this pattern. You're putting in dock-to-dark hours for a handful of fish in that mid-20s-inch range with the occasional better one mixed in, but that's the trade you make in late July heat. Daytime drifting on the flats is close to dead right now for bass — don't waste the tide on it.

Where the daylight bite is actually productive is bluefish, and that's been the story all month. We flagged this pattern last week — said the blitz would hold as long as the warm, stable weather stuck around — and it has. Bunker pods are still getting worked over off Greenwich Point and up and down the Norwalk Islands string, especially on the last two hours of the incoming when the tide pins the bait against the rocks. Topwater poppers and 2-ounce Deadly Dicks worked fast through the froth are doing the damage. Get there early — by 8 or 9 a.m. the weekend boat traffic through that stretch turns the blitzes into a demolition derby, and the fish scatter the second three center consoles converge on the same slick.

Fluke has softened up the way it always does once the shallow water gets uncomfortable. The open-flat drift off the Norwalk Islands that produced all June has gone quiet — those fish have pushed into the channel edges and deeper cuts around Sheffield Island, 25 to 35 feet, where there's still cooler water moving. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift through the channel bend, are still turning fish, but you're covering more water for fewer bites than you were a month ago. Structure-oriented fluke fishing now, not flat-water fluke fishing.

Black sea bass are holding up as the most dependable bottom bite on the beat. Cockenoe Reef and the outer rockpile at Penfield Reef, 20 to 30 feet, squid strips or clam belly on a bucktail teaser rig, bounced right on the structure — that fishery hasn't slowed a bit through the heat. Porgies are thick on the Cows off Stamford, 20 to 35 feet on those humps, sandworms and clam on a high-low rig. That's about as close to a sure thing as this beat has right now — light tackle, steady action, good for a kid's first trip or a slow afternoon when the bass game isn't worth the gas.

One thing I'll say plainly: don't bother with blackfish right now. The Cows and Penfield hold good tog structure, but this is the dead zone for that fishery — they're scattered and uninterested until the water starts to turn in October. Save the crab and green crab money for fall.

Boat traffic is the other variable I'm playing chess with every trip. Weekends through the Norwalk Islands are a circus by mid-morning — wake after wake rolling through the cuts, pushing bait and fish off the structure. If you can only fish Saturday or Sunday, be on the water at first light and off by 9, or wait for the evening tide when the marina crowd thins out. Weekday mornings are still clean.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full in early August, which should sharpen up the current through Sheffield Island channel and around Cockenoe's east end — stronger tide, tighter bite windows, but better odds when you hit it right. If the warm, stable pattern holds like it has, I expect the bluefish blitzes to keep pushing along the beachfront and the bass to stay locked into their after-dark rhythm. I wouldn't change my program: reef structure at night for stripers, moving tide for everything else, and an early alarm clock on the weekends.
